You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Storm, tempest

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, the storm or tempest most commonly symbolizes divine judgment and the wrath of God — an overwhelming manifestation of God's power breaking in upon human sin and rebellion. Closely bound to this is the theophanic sense: the storm as the vehicle or accompaniment of God's presence and speech. In devotional and homiletical use, the storm is also very widely applied to the trials, tribulations, and chaos of life that test faith, from which Christ delivers believers — an application anchored in the Gospel accounts of Jesus calming the storm.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Nahum 1:3 — 'The LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm'",
    "Jeremiah 23:19 and 30:23 — the whirlwind/tempest of the LORD going forth in fury upon the wicked",
    "Isaiah 29:6 — visitation of the LORD with storm and tempest and devouring fire",
    "Isaiah 28:2 — a destroying storm as the instrument of judgment",
    "Ezekiel 13:11-13 — a stormy wind rending the false prophets' whitewashed wall in God's fury",
    "Jonah 1:4-15 — the great tempest sent by the LORD because of Jonah's flight",
    "Psalm 83:15 — 'persecute them with thy tempest'",
    "Job 38:1 — the LORD answering Job out of the whirlwind (theophany)",
    "Psalm 29 — the voice of the LORD in the thunderstorm",
    "Psalm 107:23-30 — the LORD raising and stilling the stormy wind at sea",
    "Mark 4:35-41 (with Matthew 8:23-27; Luke 8:22-25) — Jesus rebuking the wind and calming the sea",
    "Matthew 7:24-27 — the house on the rock withstanding wind, rain, and floods"
  ],

      ],
      "prominence": "dominant"
    },

        "Exodus 19:16-19",
        "Ezekiel 1:4",
        "2 Kings 2:11"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {

      "basis": [

        "Mark 4:39-41 read against Psalm 107"
      ],

      "basis": [

      "prominence": "minority"

    {
      "meaning": "Allegorical ecclesial reading (patristic/medieval): the boat in the storm as the Church tossed by persecution and heresy, with Christ asleep testing faith",

  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Storm/tempest is a well-established, multivalent biblical image with a recognizable consensus core: it signifies God's overwhelming power, applied chiefly as judgment/wrath in prophetic texts and as theophany in poetic texts. The 'storms of life' application dominates popular preaching, while academic scholarship emphasizes the chaos-mastery motif behind the Gospel sea-calming narratives. These strands are complementary rather than competing; interpreters generally treat context as determining which sense governs. No major tradition assigns the storm a fixed single technical meaning (unlike, e.g., leaven or the lamb), so consensus is on a cluster of related senses centered on divine power/judgment and testing."
}

      "basis": [

  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "medium",
  "notes": "There is no single settled symbolic meaning applicable to every biblical storm. Prophetic references most characteristically use storm imagery for divine judgment, while preaching and devotional interpretation often treats storms as life’s trials. Narrative, poetic, and theophanic contexts can instead emphasize chaos, deliverance, or God’s presence and power."
}

No single fixed symbolic meaning dominates across all Christian traditions or scholarly biblical studies."

BOOK ENTRY
The nations in turmoil — the raging sea, stilled at Christ's word, “Peace, be still”.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: divine judgment, and the trials of life which Christ has power to calm.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Ps 65:7; Isa 17:12-13; Mark 4:39; Luke 21:25) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Psalms 65:7 — Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people.
Isaiah 17:12 — Woe to the multitude of many people, which make a noise like the noise of the seas; and to the rushing of nations, that make a rushing like the rushing of mighty waters!
Isaiah 17:13 — The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but God shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind.
Mark 4:39 — And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
Luke 21:25 — And there shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars; and upon the earth distress of nations, with perplexity; the sea and the waves roaring;

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
